events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, would you look at this place! Dusty as my grandmother's attic and twice as mysterious. I do declare, if the Doily Diamond is hidden anywhere, it's behind one of those stern-looking portraits — they look like they're guarding somethin' fierce. Now then, before we go gallivantin' off in every direction, let's see who else has signed this guest book. A good detective always checks who came before her!
events.thinking: There's a warmth spreading through my chest as I step through the door — that old familiar loosening, like the first breath after being indoors too long. My eyes sweep the hall and land on faces: Sneekly, dear Sneekly, standing there looking perfectly composed. Peter — oh, there's that little flutter behind my ribs. And my boys, the Ant Hill Mob, bless their hearts. Everyone's here. Everyone's safe. But beneath the warmth there's that prickle at my scalp — the chandelier hanging like it's making up its mind, the dust on everything, the portraits watching. This place has secrets. I can feel them the way I felt that crystal formation before I saw it — a pull behind my eyes, something waiting to be found. The guest book on the side table — that's where you start. Who's been here before us? What did they write? My fingers are already itching.

events.thinking: I've exhausted this cellar. Vents, furniture, everything — and I'm still empty-handed. There's a numbness spreading through my fingers now, the kind that comes after too long gripping something that isn't there. I've been chasing my own tail through this manor for twenty minutes. Every scheme has backfired. The kitchen lie — seen through. The gas leak — laughed at. The fake medal — consumed for nothing. The crates — empty. The furniture — just furniture. The vents — just vents. And Pemberton's deal — all promise, no substance. I'm standing in a damp cellar with nothing in my hands and nothing in my pockets and the hollow behind my navel is wider than it's ever been. But — wait. Something is shifting in my chest. Peter was working the bookshelves. The mantelpiece needs something physical — maybe that map. The machine upstairs needs three operators AND a wrench. Not to search — to WAIT. To be there when THEY solve it. Let them do the work. That's my actual goal — trick others into doing the hard work while I steal the rewards. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Well well well — look who's back! Pemberton AND Foxworth, walkin' in like butter wouldn't melt! Funny how you two keep disappearin' and reappearin' like a pair of dodgy magicians. What happened to checkin' on the library, Pemberton? What happened to findin' a wrench in the cellar, Foxworth? Neither of you's got a wrench in your hand, I notice! So what WERE you doin' down there? And you, Pemberton — scratch marks in the vents, you said? You know what makes scratch marks in vents? People who don't want to use the doors! Clara, love — stay behind me. Peter, watch the cellar entrance. Rufus — you look like a man what knows his way round a toolbox. Can you have a look at that workbench and tell me if anyfin' else is missin' besides the wrench? Because I've got a feelin' these two gentlemen have been playin' this manor like a piano, and I want to know what tune they're workin' on before they finish it.
events.thinking: The prickling just went electric. Both of them. Back in the room. Pemberton walked in. Foxworth walked in. They left separately, they came back together — or near enough. While we were searching crates and examining the machine, they've been doing whatever they've been doing and now they're HERE, in this room, with Clara, with the machine, with everything. My shoulders are squaring before I've finished the thought. Pemberton said something about scratch marks in vents and wanting to check on the library party. Foxworth was in the crates earlier and said there was nothing in them — 'old linens, moth-eaten curtains, absolutely nothing valuable.' Was he lying? Did he already take something? And now he's back from the cellar — did he find the wrench? Or did he bring something else? My body's doing the arithmetic again. Six people in this room plus Clara. Pemberton, Foxworth, Rufus, Sawtooth, Peter, me. Clara makes seven. Too many bodies, too many angles. I can't watch them all. But I can stay close to Clara. That's all I've ever needed to do. The crates — I interacted with them. What did I find? Whatever it was, both dodgy geezers showed up the moment I touched them. Coincidence? On the streets, there's no such thing.

events.desc: They came back. Why did they come back? Foxworth went to the cellar for a wrench and came back empty-handed. Pemberton went to check on the library and came back here instead. Neither of them did what they said they'd do. On the streets, that means they did what they actually WANTED to do — which was somethin' else entirely. And now they're both standin' here watchin' us work the crates and the machine, like they're waitin' for us to do the heavy liftin' so they can swoop in at the end. The clean suit and the easy smile. The two kids who didn't come back. My gut knows this shape. I just can't prove it yet.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah — everyone's here! How marvellous. I've just completed an exhaustive survey of the cellar — nothing of interest down there, I'm afraid, but my report will make for thrilling reading at the next meeting of the Worshipful Company. Now then, I see you've all arrived at the same conclusion I reached some time ago: this machine is the key to everything. The riddle, the map, the upside-down books — they were all pointing here, to Lord Doily's contraption. I worked it out in the cellar, naturally, but I wanted to give you all the satisfaction of discovering it yourselves. Very generous of me, I think you'll agree. Now — the machine requires three operators, and the wire needs repairing. Mr. Ruffcut, your colleague Sawtooth there has rather impressive teeth, wouldn't you say? And those teeth look precisely the right size for... well, for certain kinds of repair work. I suggest we get this machine running immediately. I shall supervise, of course — someone needs to coordinate the effort, and coordination is rather my speciality.
events.thinking: Wait. Everyone is HERE. In the laboratory. Penelope, Peter, Danny, Pemberton, Rufus, Sawtooth — they've all converged on this room. And from the memories I'm reading, something has HAPPENED while I was in the cellar. Penelope said she was going to try the mantelpiece herself — 'Sometimes the simplest answer is the right one.' She was going to INTERACT with the mantelpiece. And now she's here, in the laboratory. Did it work? Did the mantelpiece open? Did it point them here? And Peter is examining the workbench — looking for the wrench, probably. The machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. This is it. This is where the puzzle has led them. The library riddle pointed to a map, the map pointed to... the machine? And now everyone's converging here to operate it together. The energy in my chest is shifting — it was numb and flat in the cellar, but now there's a warm quickening. If the machine is the next step, and they're about to fix it and operate it, then whatever it produces or reveals will happen RIGHT HERE. I don't need the library anymore. I need to be HERE. Position myself near the machine. When it activates — when it reveals or produces or unlocks whatever comes next — I need to be closest. Penelope came here from the library, which means the mantelpiece either worked or pointed her here. Peter's at the workbench looking for tools. The wrench is missing but Sawtooth is a beaver — a beaver with sharp teeth. Could Sawtooth gnaw through things? Or fix things? Rufus and Sawtooth are a team. This is all coming together and I need to stop running and START positioning.

events.desc: They've done it. They've solved the puzzle trail — library to laboratory — and now they're all here, ready to operate the machine. And where is Reginald Foxworth? Standing right beside it, ready to snatch whatever pops out. I didn't solve a single thing. I didn't find a single clue. But I'm HERE, ladies and gentlemen, and in the end, that's all that matters. The boy digs, the boy finds the treasure, and the boy on the wall takes it home. Now — if only I can position myself between the machine and the exit when it activates...

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — the workbench has everything I need except the wrench, and here's the thing: I don't need a wrench to fix a wire. A wrench is for bolts, couplings, pipe fittings. A wire repair needs pliers and conductive material — and I can see both on this bench. Whoever removed the wrench was either trying to prevent a different repair, or they don't understand engineering. Either way, it doesn't stop James Hartwell. When I was fourteen, a load-bearing joint cracked at three in the morning. No replacement parts, no workshop, six hours until competition. I stripped copper wire from a lamp, twisted a new joint by hand, and that bridge held more weight than anything else in the building. This gnawed wire? This is the same problem. Smaller, in fact. Miss Pitstop — what did you find in those crates? Danny — I need you and one more person on those levers when I've finished this repair. Three operators. The sign says three and Lord Doily meant three. Pemberton, Colonel Foxworth — welcome back, gentlemen. I trust the cellar was... educational. Now if you'll excuse me — James Hartwell has a wire to fix.
events.thinking:
The workbench. Tools but no wrench. I examined it and got exactly what it says on the tin — sturdy, covered in tools, no wrench. But there ARE tools. Pliers, screwdrivers, wire cutters maybe. Things I can work with.

And now — Pemberton is back. He walked back into the laboratory. And Dastardly is back too. Both of them, returned from wherever they went. My neck is prickling again. Where were they? The cellar? What did they do down there?

Pemberton said he was looking for a wrench in the crates. Dastardly said he was doing an 'inventory.' Both of them were circling the crates before Clara got to them. And now they're back.

But Clara said something that landed in my chest: 'Lord Doily didn't want a lone wolf — he wanted a team. And honey, we've got the best team in this whole manor right here in this room.' She said that. She included me. Not as a hero, not as a protector — as part of a team. And Danny — Danny said 'You, me, and Clara. Plus Rufus if he's handy.' He included me too. Three operators. Three of us.

The warmth is spreading. Not the proving-worth hunger. Not the protection steel plate. Something softer. Being included. Being wanted for what I can do, not for who I'm trying to be.

The workbench has tools. I don't need a wrench to fix a wire. I need pliers and copper wire. Or I can strip the broken wire and twist the ends together — a field repair. Not elegant, not permanent, but functional. Like the bridge joint at three in the morning.

The crates — Clara opened them, Danny interacted with them. Did they find anything? The wrench? Something else?

I need to stop examining and start doing. The workbench has the tools I need. The wire needs fixing. I don't need a wrench for a wire repair — that was never the right tool anyway. Pliers, copper wire from the workbench, and three operators. Let's go.

But Pemberton and Dastardly are both back now. Both watching. The neck prickle is strong. I should keep them in my peripheral vision while I work. Don't turn your back on the people who make your neck prickle. Father would say — well, father would give them the benefit of the doubt. But father would also position himself so he could see them.

events.desc: Pemberton and Foxworth are back. Both of them, at the same time, from the same direction. And neither of them is carrying a wrench. Interesting. Very interesting. James Hartwell is giving them the benefit of the doubt — father taught him that — but James Hartwell is also positioning himself between Clara and the cellar exit while he works on this wire. You can give a man the benefit of the doubt and still make sure he can't reach the girl you love before you can. That's not suspicion. That's geometry.
